  full queue answers 429 with `Retry-After`). Routes: `POST /v1/linecaster/{step}` (the image and the transcription
  so far in, the transcription with its part and the call's annotator added out; both `linecaster.page/6`
  annotation sets), `GET /v1/models`, `/health` (`status` and `protocol`, the transcription format:
  `linecaster.page/6`) and vLLM-shaped `/metrics` (the gauges saturate reads). A `Served` client asks a server that
  already answers for its `protocol` when it warms up and refuses one that names another format or none
  (`ServerError`): both sides run the same linecaster version. Built-in engines are not served: they run in the pipeline's process.
- **VLMs** run behind OpenAI-compatible servers (vLLM, SGLang, hosted endpoints): `PageRecognizer` and
  `RegionRecognizer` on the `Chat` backend, on `/v1/chat/completions`, served only. `PageRecognizer` also runs a
  **page engine** (an engine whose unit is the page) on the `InProcess` or `Served` backend: a vendor's package in
  the worker (Indra OCR), a vendor's package attached to a vLLM server (Surya OCR), or a client of a vendor's page
  pipeline behind its own HTTP API (Falcon-OCR, OXR). A VLM is a catalog preset
  (engine `chat.v1`; its data: revision, prompt, sampling, serve block) plus an adapter in
  `linecaster.engines.chat.ADAPTERS` (its code: the request, the parsing; `chat_model(<preset>)`).
- **Servers inside a task** (one GPU per HF Job): the server components `EngineServer` (`linecaster serve`) and
  `VLMServer` (vLLM or SGLang) start the server through saturate's `Engine` and go last in the pipeline,
  after the writer: datatrove chains generators, and only the last one lives until every page is written. Each
  task starts its own servers. `EngineServer(script=...)` starts a pipeline script's `serve` with
  `uv run --script`. `VendorServer` starts the **service** a page preset's `serve` block names: `vllm serve` on the
  pinned checkpoint (fetched and checked) for an engine package that attaches to vLLM, or a vendor image's entrypoint
  (with the weights downloaded to the folder it reads first), ready once its health URLs answer; it runs without the
  pipeline's environment, in the image's own. A vendor's entrypoint listens on the image's fixed ports: one service
  per machine.

## Engines

An engine is a class with a versioned id ([catalog](catalog.md#engines)). Engine packages live in
`engines/<engine>/`, each its own package: `linecaster-kraken`, `linecaster-paddlex`, `linecaster-tesseract`, the
page engines' `linecaster-indra`, `linecaster-surya` and `linecaster-services` (the clients of Falcon-OCR's and OXR's
services), and the importer `linecaster-mediawiki` (MediaWiki wikitext through wikitextprocessor). An
engine class (`<Provider><Step>Engine`) has `engine_id` (the entry point's name in `linecaster.engines`), `step`,
`capabilities` (unit, produces), an `Options` model (its keyword arguments; a preset's `weights` besides), `load()`
and `__call__(image, transcription, **params) -> Transcription` (the page image as an RGB array, or the image file's
bytes for an engine whose `image_input` is `"bytes"`, and the transcription so far, returned with its part added);
an importer (step `import`) is called with a source document (`SourceFile`) and returns a new transcription. Engines with weights load exactly the pin (`weights`,
`linecaster.catalog.fetch`). PaddleX's models load from the pinned snapshot (`create_predictor(model_dir=...)`);
`small-models-for-glam/kraken-blla-base` (the BLLA base model of September 2026) is pinned in
`linecaster_kraken.models`, and no engine uses it. Engine packages carry code only; their presets and models are in
linecaster's catalog. They import from linecaster only `linecaster.data` and the engine API
(`linecaster.engines.api`: the `Engine` protocol, `Capabilities`, the weight helpers, and for importers `Importer`,
`conventions`, `HtmlConverter`, `SourceMap`), have versions of their own
with a range of linecaster releases, and their tests in `engines/<engine>/tests/` ([catalog](catalog.md#engines)).

## Tests

`uv run pytest` runs the core's tests, one after the other; `uv run pytest -n auto` (pytest-xdist, in the `dev`
group) runs them on every core. Tests marked `gpu` or `network` (`linecaster.testing.markers`: `gpu`, `network`,
`slow`; `--strict-markers`) skip where the device or the network is missing. The CI workflow
(`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, CPU only, no secrets, uv's cache kept between runs) runs `uv sync --locked
--all-extras` (the extras' readers are tested and documented too), `uv run pytest -n auto -m "not gpu and not
network"`, `linecaster catalog verify`, `linecaster docs` and the site's strict build (the generated
pages are not in git, so CI writes them and a broken reference in them fails the build). The docs workflow
(`.github/workflows/docs.yml`) writes them too and publishes the site, built by Zensical, with mike (Zensical's fork) on the `gh-pages` branch, which GitHub Pages serves
(`https://storytracer.github.io/linecaster/`): a release tag `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` as version `<major>.<minor>`,
with `latest` (the site's default) moved to it; nothing else is published. The engines' environments are too large for it
(torch): their tests (`engines/<engine>/tests/`) and the PEP 723 test
scripts (`tests/test_engines_catalog.py`, `tests/test_page_engines_catalog.py`, `tests/test_line_recognizers.py`) run locally. Every built-in engine and every public
component passes the conformance checks of `linecaster.testing` (`check_engine`: the engine protocol; `check_component`:
the contract against what the component does to sample pages, `to_dict()`, pickling, `warm_up()`, failed pages).

An engine package's tests run in an environment that has the engine: `uv run tests/test_engines_catalog.py
engines/<engine>/tests`. `tests/test_engines_catalog.py` holds kraken, PaddleX and Tesseract for the catalog's
line-recognizer presets.

## Recipe scripts

A catalog recipe is YAML (`src/linecaster/catalog/data/recipes/<id>.yaml`: its presets and options; its hash in
the index). Its
environment and entry point is a uv script of its own, `recipes/<id>.py`: a PEP 723 block with `linecaster[ray]`
and exactly the engine packages its presets need (recipe → presets → engines → packages:
`linecaster.catalog.code.recipe_packages`), its lock, and a body that only calls
`linecaster.execution.run.recipe(__file__, "<id>")`, which runs the recipe through its pipeline template with `--recipe`
set. The pipeline scripts depend on no model choice (`pipelines/transcribe_modular.py` has PaddleX and Tesseract);
the recipes bring theirs (`recipes/squiddle.py`: kraken and PaddleX).

The recipe scripts take linecaster and its engine packages from the `main` branch on GitHub, so a script runs from
its URL with no checkout (`uv run https://raw.githubusercontent.com/storytracer/linecaster/main/recipes/squiddle.py
IMAGES OUT`, `hf jobs uv run <URL> ...`) as well as from one (`uv run recipes/squiddle.py`, `uv run launch.py
squiddle`). A run from the URL resolves the header afresh, and its run record names the script `recipes/<id>.py`
(uv runs a temporary copy); a run from a checkout uses the script's lock, whose linecaster commit moves when it is
relocked. Their HF Jobs need no `--commit`: `jobs.dependencies` installs
linecaster from `main` with the lock's versions as constraints. With `--endpoint` the served engines need not be
installed in the client's environment. To preview the site from a checkout: `uv run linecaster docs`, then `uv run --group docs
zensical serve`.

## Pipeline scripts

There are no environment folders: a pipeline is a self-contained uv script in `pipelines/` (a PEP 723 block, a
`<script>.py.lock` next to it, `uv run <script>`) that runs one pipeline template with slots, one script per template,
never one per machine. The template is library code, `linecaster.templates.<name>` (its options, engines, components,
pipeline id and slots), so a downstream project's script can run it in its own environment with its own defaults
([pipelines](pipelines.md#pipeline-templates)):

| Script | Pipeline id | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `harvest.py` | `harvest.v1` | downloads page images (and a library's OCR, manifests) once into item folders, plus page records |
| `transcribe_modular.py` | `transcribe_modular.v1` | lines and a recognizer, optionally layout, tables, formulas, then post-processing; every step a preset the user picks; PaddleX and Tesseract, no kraken |
| `transcribe_vlm.py` | `transcribe_vlm.v1` | a VLM per page or per layout region |
| `transcribe_page.py` | `transcribe_page.v1` | a page engine per page, with the service its preset names |
| `bind.py` | `bind.v1` | item texts and item documents from page records |
| `convert.py` | `convert.v1` | page images converted to JPEG, JPEG 2000, PNG or WebP by an image preset, on NVIDIA GPUs where the machine has them |
| `import_transcriptions.py` | `import_transcriptions.v1` | transcriptions in any format read into page records by an importer, a ground truth by default |
| `score.py` | `score.v1` | page records scored against a ground truth under a benchmark |

`linecaster.execution.run.main` gives every pipeline the same command line: `--on local|ray|hf-jobs`, `--backend
in-process|served`, `--endpoint` (a running server), `serve` (`linecaster serve` with the script's models), `ray`
(Ray's CLI from the script's environment). Slots have no default presets: every slot is picked, or a recipe fills
them (`--recipe`); `launch.py` runs a recipe or a page preset by name ([catalog](catalog.md#pipelines-recipes-and-launchpy)).
Each script's page in the [catalog's docs](../catalog/README.md) lists its slots and options.

Script environments: the repository is not a uv workspace (engine pins conflict). A script lists what it needs
itself: linecaster with the extra every pipeline uses (`ray` for `--on ray` and `ray start`) and its engine
packages (`convert.py` and the transcription scripts also `nvimgcodec`: NVIDIA's GPU codecs, used where the machine has a GPU); `s3://` paths need no extra (the core
installs datatrove's `s3` extra, s3fs). A source is
declared by the package that needs it, and `uv lock` applies the sources of path and git dependencies too:
the kraken fork by `linecaster-kraken`, and `stubs/opencv-contrib-python` (the
headless build of the version PaddleX pins; one cv2) by `linecaster-paddlex`. `tests/test_scripts.py` checks
sources, locks and wheels for both machines (uv's `required-environments` does not work in scripts).

torch is never a dependency of the core. Only `linecaster-kraken` pins it (`torch==2.14.0`: kraken's upper bound is
`<=2.14`, and the PyPI 2.14 wheels are the CUDA 13 build on Linux, aarch64 and x86_64), and only environments with
`linecaster-kraken` are bound by that pin; the others take what their own dependencies allow. Each lock's torch is
fixed in `tests/test_scripts.py` (`TORCH`), so it changes only on purpose:

| Environment | torch | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_engines_catalog.py` | 2.14.0 | `linecaster-kraken`'s pin |
| `pipelines/transcribe_page.py`, `tests/test_page_engines_catalog.py` | 2.14.0 | surya-ocr's (`>=2.7,<3`), not pinned: the version it was locked at |
| `tools/cuda_probe.py` | 2.14.0 | its own pin: it probes the CUDA build of `linecaster-kraken`'s torch on a Jobs host |
| `pipelines/transcribe_modular.py`, `transcribe_vlm.py`, `harvest.py`, `bind.py`, `convert.py`, `launch.py`, `tests/test_line_recognizers.py`, linecaster's own (`uv.lock`) | none | no engine there needs it |

## Executors and Jobs

| `--on` | Executor |
|---|---|
| `local` | datatrove's `LocalPipelineExecutor` |
| `ray` | `RayGPUExecutor` for stages with servers and single-stage pipelines with engines (each task holds one GPU; without `--tasks`, 4 tasks per GPU of the cluster, and one per GPU where each task starts a VLM's server, which takes minutes), `RayExecutor` (datatrove's `RayPipelineExecutor`) otherwise, on CPUs (an item stage, a harvest; extra `[ray]`); both stop the run at an error that is not the pages', fail a launch that left tasks unfinished, and check first that a live node can run a task |
| `hf-jobs` | `JobsExecutor`: datatrove's `JobsPipelineExecutor` with JSON-lines logs; `GPUJobsExecutor` for multi-GPU flavors |

datatrove's `JobsPipelineExecutor` is experimental and dill-pickles the pipeline, so the launching machine and the
Jobs run the same Python minor version (3.12). `uv run` outside a project drops `[tool.uv.sources]`:
`linecaster.execution.jobs.dependencies(commit, script)` spells out a pipeline's dependencies and sources as URLs, the
installed packages' own sources from the script's lock (the commit must be pushed), and pins every other package at
the lock's version; each Job runs a uv script that carries the pins and the script's overrides, which `uv run --with`
would ignore ([pipelines](running.md#hf-jobs-helpers)).

Workers that share something beyond their tasks (a proxy list, whose proxies each worker may use only while no other
does) agree through the [broker](broker.md), a folder any executor's workers can reach, on any storage datatrove
supports: leases say who holds what, marks what is unavailable until when, and a worker is a slot of its machine that
outlives the processes (on Ray every task is one) that take it over.

## The run layout

One job is one pipeline for one batch on one executor; resume is datatrove's, per task, so tasks stay small. A
pipeline reads the previous folder and writes complete page records with one more part filled in:

| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|
| `originals/` | the delivered images and files; never modified |
| `OUT/pages/` | page records (`PageJsonlWriter`, `PageParquetWriter`), bucketed by item id: a whole item in one file, so no joins |
| `OUT/rejects/` | every page that carries errors (`RejectWriter`, put before the first writer by the builder): key, field, error, raw value |
| `OUT/logs/` | datatrove's completion markers, logs and stats; `OUT/logs/broker/`, the [broker](broker.md) by default |
| `OUT/traces/` | the traces ([tracing](tracing.md)) |
| `OUT/run.yaml` | the run record ([pipelines](pipelines.md#the-run-record)) |
| `OUT/sample.parquet` | the sample a run read, one row per page in sample order ([pipelines](running.md#samples)) |
| `OUT/manifests/` | the manifests a sample read (with `sample.jsonl`), or a harvest saved |

`PageRecordReader` reads page records of linecaster's writers, fetching images again by URI (`uri_map` for local
copies). Checks like `PageValidator` record on the page why it failed.

**Readers** follow datatrove's conventions (`BaseDiskReader`: `data_folder`, `paths_file`, `glob_pattern`,
`limit`/`skip` per task; files distributed over tasks in turn, Parquet tables by rows in equal shards,
`linecaster.components.readers.tables`, so a table needs no splitting): `ImageFolderReader` (image files),
`ImageParquetReader` (an image column: bytes, an HF image struct or a path), `ManifestReader` (IIIF or METS, parsed
by `linecaster.formats.manifests`, its files fetched through `linecaster.net.http`; a manifest,
or a row of a Parquet item table, is an entry, so an item stays in one task; a IIIF Collection entry is its
manifests, one level; `existing_ocr` fetches a library's OCR as a document media, which a `TranscriptionConverter`
reads as `ocr_original`, the builder adding one when missing), `PdfReader` (PDF files as items, pages rendered with
pypdfium2, extra `[pypdfium2]`) and `PageRecordReader`. Readers that fetch over http(s) request ahead in a window
that grows while no request waits for the rate limits (`linecaster.net.http.prefetched`), through one fetcher per
process and configuration, so the limits hold across a worker's tasks; `ImageParquetReader` and `ManifestReader`
suggest a task count from their input (`auto_tasks`), which a pipeline without engines runs with
([pipelines](running.md#tasks-workers-and-rate-limits)).

**The workflow** is harvest → transcribe → bind: `pipelines/harvest.py` downloads images (and OCR, manifests) once
into item folders plus page records, the transcribe pipelines read those with `--pages`, `pipelines/bind.py` makes
item texts and documents. An item's pages can land in different tasks; item-level steps are a second stage over item
shards (`--item-shards N` writes `OUT/pages/<shard>/<rank>`, `pipelines/bind.py` reads whole shards), as datatrove's
own multi-stage pipelines read per-bucket folders ([pipelines](pipelines.md#the-item-stage)).

<!-- docs/reference/pipelines.md -->

# Pipelines: contracts and the builder

A pipeline is a list of components (datatrove `PipelineStep`s) and composites. Before it runs, the builder
(`linecaster.execution.builder`) checks the components' contracts, expands the composites, and cuts the pipeline into
stages. Every pipeline script goes through it (`linecaster.execution.run`). Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s.

## Contracts

Every component returns its contract from `contract()` (`linecaster.core.contract`):

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Part:
    name: str                  # a name of PARTS, or "*" (every part)
    transcription: str | None  # ocr_new, ocr_original, ...; None: page-level (image, metadata, transcription_file)
                               # or the item record's

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Contract:
    unit: str                  # "page", "item" (what the input stream carries) or "any" (servers)
    unit_out: str | None       # set when the component changes the stream's unit (binder: page -> item, splitter: back)
    reads: frozenset[Part]
    adds: frozenset[Part]
    replaces: frozenset[Part]
    removes: frozenset[Part]   # parts the component does not pass on (gone for every later component)
    kind: str                  # reader, writer, server, model, transform, binder, splitter, validator, composite
```

- **The vocabulary** is `PARTS` in `linecaster.catalog.schema`: `image`, `metadata` and `transcription_file` (a
  library's own transcription delivered with the page, as a document media) (page-level), what presets produce (`PRODUCES`: `regions`, `reading_order`, `lines`, `baselines`, `text`, `words`, `word_confidences`,
  `line_confidences`, `tables`, `formulas`, `markdown`, `html`, `doctags`, `layout_json`, `latex`), and
  `line_regions`, `hierarchy`, `paragraphs`, `document`. A part is written `transcription:name` (`ocr_new:lines`);
  `ocr_original:*` is every part of a transcription.
- **Simple components** declare class attributes (`unit`, `role`, `parts_read`, `parts_added`, `parts_replaced`,
  `parts_removed`) that
  the default `contract()` of `Contracted` reads; page-level names stay page-level, the others belong to the
  component's `transcription`. Components whose parts depend on their options compute `contract()`.
- **Model components** read the page image (recognition also `lines`, tables and formulas `regions`) and add their
  preset's `capabilities.produces`: the preset of the `InProcess` backend (`preset`), of the `Served` backend
  (`preset`, set by `runtime.run.engines`) or of the `Chat` backend; without a preset the engine class's
  `capabilities` (read from its source in the repository, else from the class); without either the step's default.
  The chat recognizers add `text` too, `RegionRecognizer` also `lines` (and replaces `lines` and `text`: the
  transcription's earlier lines are replaced).
- **Readers** add `image` and `metadata`; `ManifestReader(existing_ocr=True)` also `transcription_file`, which the
  `TranscriptionConverter` reads (adding `ocr_original:*`);
  `PageRecordReader` what `provides=` declares (`["ocr_new:lines", ...]`), or anything (`*`, reads after it are
  not checked) when it declares nothing. With `fetch_images=False` it brings no `image`.
- **Writers** read what they write and add nothing (`ImageFilesWriter` replaces `metadata`: the image's URI then
  names its copy; `PageFileWriter`: `lines` for hOCR, ALTO and PAGE, `text` for
  md and txt, `document` for HTML and JSON, `image` for plots). **Servers** have role `server` and unit
  `any`.
- **The `ItemAssembler`** changes the unit from pages to items, the **`ItemSplitter`** back: an item record holds its page
  records, so what the pages carried stays available across either (the checks carry the parts over), apart from
  the page image's bytes (`image`: an item record has none) at the binder and the item's `document` at the splitter.
- **Item-unit components** (`ParagraphBuilder(unit="item")`, `DocumentComposer(unit="item")`)
  read item records: one datatrove document per item, `doc.metadata["item"]` holding the item id and its page records
  in order (`linecaster.core.item`); they read and add the parts of the pages' transcriptions, the item
  `DocumentComposer` adds the item's `document` next to the record. **Item writers** (`ItemDocumentWriter`, `ItemTextWriter`)
  read the `document` and write it by each text's transcription strategy.
  `RecipeStamper` has unit `any`: before an item writer it stamps the pages of each item record.
- A step without a contract (a plain datatrove step) passes pages and touches no part.

| Component | Reads | Adds | Replaces, removes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LineAssigner` | `lines`, `regions` | `line_regions` | `regions`, `reading_order`, `lines` |
| `HierarchyDetector` | `regions`, `lines` | `hierarchy` | `regions`, `lines` |
| `ParagraphBuilder` | `regions`, `lines` | `paragraphs` | `paragraphs` (made anew where they exist) |
| `DocumentComposer` | `regions`, `lines` (and `paragraphs` when there are) | `document` (rendered, not stored; no annotator) | |
| `Tagger` | `regions`, `lines` (the model tagger: `image` and its targets, regions or lines) | `tags` | |
| `ImageFetcher` | `metadata` | | `image` |
| `ImageConverter` | `metadata` | | `metadata` (with `keep_bytes` also `image`; without it removes `image`) |
| `TranscriptionConverter` | `metadata`, `transcription_file` (with `source="media"`) | `<transcription>:*` | |
| `RecipeStamper` | | | |

## Component shapes

- **Per-unit transform** (`shape = "unit"`): `process_page(doc, page) -> page | None`; `PageComponent` owns the loop
  and the stats. In-process model components have this shape.
- **Stream transform** (`shape = "stream"`): overrides `run(data)` and yields each page when it is done, possibly
  out of order (served model components, `PageRecognizer`, `RegionRecognizer`). It reports what happens to each page
  inside it with `notify(doc, event)`: `prepare` when a request is built, `done` when its result came back. The
  served model components share one streaming loop (`ModelComponent`): a component names its requests (`_rows`: one per page, one
  per region for `RegionRecognizer`), builds and parses each (`_request`, `_parse`) and says which pages a finished
  one completes (`_done`).
- Only readers and writers see `rank`, `world_size` and files (a test walks every component class, with no exceptions):
  a component that rejects a page records why on the page, and the `RejectWriter` names the task's file.

## Backends

A model component's backend (`linecaster.backends`) says where its engine runs:

- `InProcess("pkg:Class", **options)` (or `InProcess.from_preset(ref)`; a model component given a preset ref,
  `LayoutDetector("single-region")`, builds one): the engine loads in the worker;
- `Served(endpoint, model=name, ...)`: `linecaster serve` (or a server speaking its routes) hosts it, reached through
  saturate on `/v1/linecaster/{step}`; `warm_up()` refuses a server whose `/health` names another transcription
  format than `linecaster.page/4`, or none;
- `Chat(preset, endpoint=None, served_name=None, max_window=32, initial_window=4, read_timeout=600.0, api_key=None,
  headers=None, prefer="page")`: a chat preset's VLM behind an OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, SGLang, a hosted
  endpoint) on `/v1/chat/completions`; `preset` is a preset ref, a model's Hugging Face id (its preset with unit
  `prefer`) or a configured adapter (`chat_model`); without an endpoint, the task's `VLMServer` on port 8000.
  `PageRecognizer(backend)` and `RegionRecognizer(backend, labels=..., pad=None)` (`pad`: the adapter's `region_pad`, else 8) take it (or a chat preset's ref).
  `Chat(..., overrides={...})` sets the chat engine's options over the preset's settings (`max_tokens`, `temperature`,
  `top_p`, `repair_max_tokens`, `repair_temperature`, `repetition_detection`; `--set recognition.<option>=<value>` in
  `pipelines/transcribe_vlm.py`, and `--no-repetition-detection` there to turn the last off: it is on by default
  where the preset's vLLM takes it); the ones that differ from the preset's are recorded with the adapter
  (`overrides`) and count in `pipeline_sha256`. With `repair_max_tokens` set, `PageRecognizer` runs the
  [repair passes](glossary.md): a page whose completion stopped at `max_tokens` waits while its repair requests go
  into the same window, one per cap while each stops at its cap, and leaves the component with every pass recorded as a
  raw output (`pass`, `kept`: the one its annotations were parsed from); `PageRecognizer(..., repair_only=True)` sends only
  the repair requests, for page records read with `PageRecordReader` (`--pages ... --repair-only`). The streaming
  loop of `ModelComponent` offers this to every served component: a finished request may ask for a second one
  (`_second_request`), whose response comes back with it (`_second_done`), and that one for another
  (`_next_request`).
  `PageRecognizer` also takes a page engine's `InProcess` or `Served` backend (or its preset's ref): a stream
  transform served, a per-unit transform in-process; it reads the page image and adds `text` and what the preset
  produces. A page engine's `endpoint` option (where its service is) is operational.

The built-in engines (`layout.single-region.v1`, the rule-based steps' and the taggers) run in the pipeline's
process only: `runtime.run.engines` keeps a preset of one in-process when the other models are served, and
`linecaster serve` refuses them.

**The `Tagger`** (`linecaster.components.tagging`) runs a tagging engine on every page, by preset or engine spec like
the rule components (`Tagger("geometry-tags")`, `Tagger(InProcess("linecaster.engines:ChatTaggingEngine",
schemes=["degraded"], panel=[...]))`, `options` over either), and adds `tags`: classifications in property schemes
([data model](data-model.md#classifications)). It decodes the page image only for an engine that reads it (the
model tagger, a client of chat servers that the run provides), and passes the page's id, which review items name.
Stats: `tagged`, `undecided`.

## The builder

```python
plan = build(components, tasks=8, until=None, after=None, taps={"LineAssigner": "OUT/taps/lines"},
             run_folder="OUT", recipe=("squiddle", "sha256:..."))
plan.check()          # PipelineConfigError listing every problem
plan.stages           # [Stage(name, tasks, components, pipeline)]: one datatrove pipeline each, run in order
plan.graph            # nodes (components; composites expanded, their group kept), edges (part -> the component reading it)
plan.mermaid()        # the graph as a Mermaid flowchart: stages and composites as subgraphs
plan.describe()       # stages with each component's contract, the edges, the problems
```

**Checks**, all collected: a stage starts with a reader; every part a component reads is added earlier in its stage
(or by the stage's reader) and not removed since (`removes`, even after a reader that provides anything); a part
is added by one component only, unless a later component declares it in `replaces`;
units fit (a page component cannot follow an item stream, an item component needs a binder before it); the parts carry
across a binder and a splitter (apart from `image` and the item's `document`); server components go last; a served model
component whose endpoint is a server component of its stage (same loopback port) finds its model in that server's list; the alternatives of a group add the same parts, sit next to each other, each with a condition,
`OTHERWISE` last; names given to `until`, `after` and `taps` fit exactly one component.

**Order** is the given one; the builder checks it and does not reorder. It inserts a `TranscriptionConverter` (into
`ocr_original`) right after a component that adds `transcription_file` when no later component reads it, the
`RecipeStamper` before the first writer when the run follows a recipe, a `RejectWriter` into
`<run_folder>/rejects` before the first writer (or binder) when there is a run folder and the pipeline has none, and moves the server components at the end into the
stage of the model components when it cuts. `build(..., max_page_errors=SHARE)` sets every page component's error budget.

**Branches**: `branch(component, when=Condition, group=None)` gives a component a condition, a picklable predicate on the
page record with a `describe()` (`MetadataEquals(key, value)`, `OTHERWISE`). The component processes the pages the
condition accepts; the others pass unchanged. Components with the same `group` are alternatives: each page goes through
the first one whose condition accepts it. A per-unit component gets its pages one by one; any other component one stream of
them, the pages it does not take passed on as it yields.

**Composites**: `Composite(name, components, contract=None)` expands into its components (nested composites too); its
outward contract is derived (what its components read that none of them adds, what they add and replace) unless given.
`ModularTranscriber(lines, recognition, layout, formulas_separately=False, transcription="ocr_new")` is layout
(`"single-region"`: the page as one region) → lines → line assignment → line recognition; each step a component, a
backend or a preset.

**Stages**: with `tasks > 1`, the first binder (a component whose stream changes from pages to items) cuts the
pipeline, unless the reader already gives each task whole items (`ManifestReader`, `PageRecordReader(item_shards=
True)`). The first stage writes its page records in item shards into `<run_folder>/pages/` (the pipeline's own
`PageJsonlWriter` there, now with `item_shards=N`, N = `tasks` unless it set its own); the second starts with
`PageRecordReader(item_shards=True, fetch_images=False)` declaring the parts the first stage added, runs the binder
and what follows, as N tasks. An `ItemSplitter` after the binder needs no cut of its own: the items are whole in the
task, so its pages are too. One stage logs to `OUT/logs/`, two to `OUT/logs/pages/` and `OUT/logs/items/`; the run
record lists the stages. Each stage gets its own executor, and the later one `depends=` on the earlier one:

| `--on` | Executors | Stages |
|---|---|---|
| `local` | `LocalPipelineExecutor` | the second starts when the first is complete |
| `ray` | `RayGPUExecutor` for stages with servers, `RayExecutor` for the item stage and pipelines without engines (CPUs only) | the same, through `depends=` |
| `hf-jobs` | `JobsExecutor` (datatrove's `JobsPipelineExecutor` with JSON-lines logs; `GPUJobsExecutor` for multi-GPU flavors on stages with servers) | consecutive launches: the second launches when the first's Jobs are complete; both on `--flavor` |

**Partial runs** (components named by their datatrove `name`, their class name, or a composite's name for its last
component):

- `until=BLOCK` (`--until`): the components up to and including BLOCK, then a `PageJsonlWriter` into
  `<run_folder>/pages` (and the server components);
- `after=BLOCK` (`--after`, with `--pages DIR`): the pipeline's `PageRecordReader`, then the components after BLOCK;
  the reader declares the parts the components up to BLOCK add;
- `taps={BLOCK: DIR}` (`--tap-after BLOCK DIR`, repeatable): a `Tap` observer writes every page record as it
  leaves BLOCK into `DIR/<rank>.jsonl.gz`.

**In this process**: `run_pages(components, docs)` checks the components and runs them on `docs` (datatrove documents) as
task 0 of 1, without an executor (a leading reader reads its own input after them); `run_plan(plan)` runs a plan's
stages that way. A pipeline script's `--page IMAGE OUT` runs its pipeline on one image like that, and `linecaster
page IMAGE OUT [--recipe R | --pipeline ID] [pipeline options]` finds the script (the recipe's pipeline, else
`transcribe_modular.v1`) and runs it so.

`--dry-run` prints the plan (`describe()` under `plan`, with the run record) and the Mermaid graph, and fails like
a run would when there are problems; a run with problems exits with code 2 before it writes anything.

## Observers

`linecaster.core.observers.Observer` has `on_task_start(rank, world_size)`, `on_warm_up(component, seconds)`,
`on_enter(component, doc)`, `on_exit(component, doc, error=None)`, `on_unit(component, doc, event, **attributes)` (from stream
components' `notify`: `prepare` and `request` in saturate's prepare threads, `request` with a `carrier` dict for the
trace context, `done` with `error`, tokens and `finish_reason`; `region` for a request per region),
`on_task_event(block, event, start_ns, end_ns, **attributes)` (from `Component.report`: a reader's `file`, a writer's
`flush`), `on_leave(doc)` (a page leaves the stage's last component), `on_task_end(error=None)` (also when the task
fails) and `environment()` (variables for a server a component starts in the task). When a stage has observers
(`build(..., observers=[...])`, taps, tracing), the builder puts a `Boundary` after every component: the boundary
between component *i* and *i + 1* calls `on_exit(i)` and `on_enter(i + 1)` for each page, so a component's time per page
includes waiting in a served window; `error` is the entry the component added to `doc.metadata["errors"]`. Boundaries
are plain callables, not datatrove steps, so they add no stats; a stage without observers has none.

Every stage with a run folder (or an OTLP endpoint) is traced: the builder adds a `linecaster.tracing.Tracing`
observer (`build(..., trace_share=SHARE)`, `--trace-share`; [tracing](tracing.md)).

## Warm-up

Every component has `warm_up()` (idempotent): engines load there (`InProcess.warm_up()`), servers start there
(`EngineServer`, `VLMServer`), a served backend reads its secrets there; components with nothing to load keep the
no-op. A component's `__call__`, which datatrove's executors call, warms it up before its `run` starts: components warm up
as the stream reaches them, the last one first (the servers before the components that call them). The time is the
component's own stat, `warm_up_seconds` (per task), and goes to the observers (`on_warm_up(component, seconds)`); a page's
measured `seconds` never include loading. An error in a warm-up fails the task (a server that does not start: a
`ServerError`).

## Failures

- **Per page.** An exception in a per-unit transform's `process_page` (other than a `PipelineConfigError`,
  `CatalogError` or `ServerError`, which fail the task) becomes an entry in the page's `doc.metadata["errors"]`:
  `{"component": class, "step": a model component's step, "preset": its id or null, "type": the exception's class,
  "error": the message}`; a failed request of a served component is the same with type `ServerError`; checks
  (`PageValidator`, `ImageConverter`) add `field` and `raw_value`. The page goes on as it was.
- **Later model components pass it by** (`skip_on_error`, the default for model components; stat `skipped_after_error`), at
  once: in-process the page leaves the component before the next one enters, served it is put straight onto the
  component's results (it never waits for the window, nor for the end of the input).
- **Rejects.** The `RejectWriter` writes every page that carries errors to `OUT/rejects/<rank>.jsonl`, one line
  per error (`key`, `field`, `error`, `raw_value`, and the entry's `component`, `step`, `preset`, `type`), and passes
  it on: the page records keep failed pages with their errors, so a later pipeline reading them passes them by too.
  `PageFileWriter(skip_failed=True)` writes no per-page files for them (the modular pipeline's `--files`), so a
  file is never what the components before the failure made of a page.
- **The error budget.** A component may fail on `max_page_errors` of a task's pages (`--max-page-errors`, default
  0.01), judged from the 100th page on: from then, more errors than `share × pages` fail the task with a
  `PageError` (with the default: two failures in the first 100 pages, three in 300). Fewer pages are too few to
  judge. datatrove reruns a failed task whole.
- **Page images** (`linecaster.images.pixels`). The model components give engines plain 8-bit RGB pixels (Pillow's
  `convert("RGB")` of the file: no ICC profile applied, no EXIF orientation), decoded once per page and process: the
  components after the first that needs a page's image use the same read-only array (stats `image_decoded`,
  `image_shared`). `--image-decode` (`ModelComponent.image_decode`, set by the builder) says how: `auto` (the default)
  decodes JPEG, JPEG 2000 and TIFF in 8-bit gray or RGB on an NVIDIA GPU where the machine has one and
  `linecaster[nvimgcodec]` is installed, the worker's GPU, everything else with Pillow; `cpu` always with Pillow;
  `gpu` like `auto`, but a machine without a GPU is an error. A served component sends its choice with the image, and
  `linecaster serve` decodes there; a chat adapter builds its request from the same pixels. A GPU and Pillow round a
  lossy image's pixels differently, so a step records its decoder (measurement `decoder`); an image a GPU refuses,
  or a GPU that fails, is decoded with Pillow (stats `gpu_decoded`, `cpu_decoded`, `gpu_decode_refused`,
  `gpu_decode_errors`). The option is operational: it is not part of `pipeline_sha256`, since `auto` depends on the
  machine anyway.
- **Errors** (`linecaster.errors`): library code raises `PipelineConfigError` (a pipeline, option or input that
  cannot work; `problems` lists them), `CatalogError`, `PageError(page_id, component)` and `ServerError`, all
  `LinecasterError`s, never `SystemExit`; the `linecaster` command and a pipeline script's `main` turn them into
  exit codes (2: nothing was launched).

## The run record

`OUT/run.yaml` (schema `linecaster.run-record/2`, the pydantic model `linecaster.execution.record.RunRecord`, JSON
Schema `catalog/schemas/run-record-2.json`) records the script, the recipe, the command line, the options, where it
ran and the software, and:

- `pipeline`: per stage its name, tasks and components in order, each component as its `to_dict()` (below) with its
  `contract`, composite, group and condition;
- `pipeline_sha256`: the hash of the pipeline's **functional** parameters.

**`to_dict()`** gives a component as it was built: `{"component": class name, "class": "module:Class", "params": {...}}`,
every constructor parameter with the value it was given or its default (`**kwargs` flattened), JSON-compatible:
backends as `{"backend": "in-process", "engine", "options", "preset", "preset_sha256"}`, `{"backend": "served",
"endpoint", "model", "max_window", ..., "preset", "engine"}` or `{"backend": "chat", "adapter", "preset",
"preset_sha256", "model", "revision", "served_name", "endpoint", "max_window", ...}` (a chat adapter's dict plus where
its server is), nested components as their dicts, secrets as `{"env": NAME}`, folders as paths, callables as `module:name`. A component
keeps the arguments it was constructed with; `live_params` names those the builder may change afterwards (a page
record reader's `provides`). A composite's dict is its group: its parameters and its components' dicts.

**Functional and operational parameters.** A parameter is *functional* when changing it can change what a run
writes for a page or an item (its page records, files and texts) or how they are partitioned (`item_shards`); it is
*operational* when it only changes where things are read and written, how the work is spread and paced, or how a
server is reached. `pipeline_sha256` covers the functional ones (`provenance.functional_pipeline`):

| Operational (left out) | Why |
|---|---|
| folders and file names: `data_folder`, `output_folder`, `output_filename`, `image_folder`, `manifest_folder`, `ocr_folder`, `folder`, `suffix`, `bucket_by_item`, `prefix` | where things are |
| which input files a task reads and how: `paths_file`, `glob_pattern`, `recursive`, `limit`, `skip`, `shuffle_files`, `batch_size` (a reader's), `http` (rate limits, the IIIF format asked for), `uri_map`, progress bars | the pages themselves are recorded per page |
| servers and clients: `port`, `host`, `python`, `script`, `vllm`, `outside_venv`, `boot_timeout`, `max_queue`, `prepare_workers`, `gpu_memory_utilization`, `extra_args`; an in-process engine's `endpoint` and `timeout` (`ENGINE_OPERATIONAL`: where its service is); a served backend's `endpoint`, `model` (the name it is hosted under, unless nothing else names its engine), `max_window`, `initial_window`, `read_timeout`, `api_key`, `headers`; a chat backend's `served_name` and the same (it counts by its adapter, preset and hash, model and revision) | how a server is started and reached |
| `name` (datatrove's display name), `compression`, `max_file_size`, `ImageConverter.keep_bytes`, `.skip_existing`, `.window`, `.initial_window`, `.max_window`, `ImageFolderReader.read_images` | presentation, file handling, memory, how many pages are in flight |
| server components (`EngineServer`, `VLMServer`, `VendorServer`) as a whole | their models count through the components they serve |
| the backend (in-process or served) | a model component counts by its engine, the engine's options and the preset with its hash, wherever it runs |

Everything else is functional: component classes and their order, transcription names, engine options, presets and
their hashes, the recipe stamp, conditions and groups, writers' formats, texts and strategies, `item_shards`. The base list
is `OPERATIONAL` in `linecaster.core.component`; a component class adds its own in `operational`. A parameter added
to a released component with a default that keeps the old behavior is left out while it has that default
(`unhashed_defaults`, e.g. `PageRecognizer`'s `repair_only`), so the pipelines that do not use it keep their hash. So a resumed run,
a run on another executor or backend, or into another folder has the same hash; another preset, option or component
has another.

**Resume.** A run into an OUT that holds a run record is checked against its newest record (`run.yaml`, or a later
`run-<time>.yaml`): another `pipeline_sha256` is refused with a `PipelineConfigError` (finished tasks would be
skipped and the folder would mix two pipelines' outputs) unless `--new-pipeline` (the new record is written next
to the earlier one and is the one the next resume is checked against); another `--tasks` is always refused (each
task would read other input), and so is another sample (the record's `sample.selected.sha256`, [samples](running.md#samples)).
The same hash, tasks and sample: a resume, as datatrove's completion markers make it.
`--dry-run` reports the same problems.

**Describe mode.** `linecaster.execution.run.describe(template, argv)` builds a pipeline template's plan in the current
process without its engines: its options parsed, presets resolved without checking that their engines are
installed, nothing loaded or started. `describe_recipe(ref)` describes a recipe that way (the template of the
recipe's pipeline id, `linecaster.templates.template(id)`, with `--recipe REF` and placeholder folders): what
`linecaster catalog index` records as the recipe's `pipeline_sha256` and `verify` compares ([catalog](catalog.md)).

## Pipeline templates

A pipeline script's code is a pipeline template in `linecaster.templates` (`harvest`, `convert`, `transcribe_modular`,
`transcribe_vlm`, `transcribe_page`, `bind`, `import_transcriptions`, `score`): its docstring (the help text), `options(ap)`, `models(a)`,
`pipeline(a, script)`, `PIPELINE` and, where recipes fill it, `SLOTS`. `linecaster.templates.templates()` lists them by
pipeline id and `template(id)` finds one; importing one imports no engine. The script in `pipelines/` is its PEP 723
block, a docstring and the call that runs the template:

```python
from linecaster.templates import transcribe_modular as template
from linecaster.execution import run

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run.main(__file__, template.__doc__, template.options, template.models, template.pipeline, template.PIPELINE,
             template.SLOTS)
```

A downstream project's script runs a shape the same way, in its own environment (the engine packages its slots need), and
may lay its own defaults over the shape's options: an `options` that calls the shape's and
then `ap.set_defaults(...)` (`--recipe` too, which `run` adds before the script's options), and a `pipeline` that
fills a default depending on other options before it calls the shape's. Its run records name its script; its
`pipeline_sha256` is the shape's for the same options.

## Importing ground truth

`pipelines/import_transcriptions.py` (`import_transcriptions.v1`) reads a source's documents into page records with
one importer (step `import`, slot `import`): a Parquet table's column holding each document (`--data-key`: a wiki
page's wikitext), a column naming a file (`--uri-key`), or the file delivered with the page; `--context-key` columns
are the document's context, `record`, `revision` and `dataset` its source's fields. Its pages are named, not read
(`ImageParquetReader(read_images=False)`, or no `--image-key`): importing needs no image. Its page records are what
`linecaster score` reads as a ground truth, and what a dataset is assembled from.

## The item stage

The item-level steps follow an `ItemAssembler`; the usual shape (`pipelines/bind.py`, and `--item-texts` of
`pipelines/transcribe_modular.py`):

```python
texts = ("literal:txt", "latin-historic+unicode-marks+flow:md")   # --text, repeatable
[PageRecordReader(pages, fetch_images=False, item_shards=True),
 ItemAssembler(),                                                  # page records -> item records
 ParagraphBuilder("unicode-paragraphs", unit="item"),        # paragraphs continued across page breaks
 DocumentComposer("linked-document", unit="item"),             # the item's document, literal
 ItemDocumentWriter(f"{out}/documents", texts=texts),     # documents/<strategy>/<item>.<ext>
 ItemTextWriter(f"{out}/texts", texts=texts)]             # texts/<strategy>.<format>/<rank>.jsonl.gz (bind: --jsonl)
```

A **text** is the item's document written by a transcription strategy in a format (`<strategy>:<format>`:
`literal` or a catalog strategy, normalizations joined by `+` too; `md`, `txt`, `html`, `json`); nothing is
normalized unless a text names a strategy, and `bind` writes only the literal document as JSON unless `--text` names
others. A JSON Lines row holds `id` (the item), `text`, `spec`, `strategy`, `strategy_sha256`, `normalizations`,
`format`, `page_ids`, `pages` and `token_count` with a token counter. The page files (`PageFileWriter`) take one
`strategy` too (`--strategy`, default `literal`).

An `ItemSplitter` after the item-level components passes each item's pages on as pages (e.g. to a `PageJsonlWriter`), with
the paragraphs made for the item.

## Page records

Stored page records are rows `{"schema": "linecaster.page/6", "id", "text", "page", "errors"}` (`PageJsonlWriter`,
`PageParquetWriter`; `PAGE_SCHEMA` in `linecaster.data.page`): `page` is the page record of the
[data model](data-model.md), its annotation sets with their annotators, raw outputs and annotations. Renderings
(the DocumentComposer's document, the files, the texts) are not part of it. `PageRecordReader` brings older rows to
today's format (`UPGRADES`, keyed by the row's `schema`, one version at a time): a `linecaster.page/4` row through
`page_4_to_5` (the derived text dropped, [data model](data-model.md#from-linecasterpage4)); a `linecaster.page/2` row through
`linecaster.data.upgrade.page_2_to_3` (field by field in the [data model](data-model.md#from-linecasterpage2)); a
`linecaster.page/1` row, whose transcriptions name their steps `model`, to page/2 first; a row without `schema` (the
oldest format) names its transcription `ocr`, read as `ocr_new`; a `.../pages` folder without records is read from
its sibling `rows/` (the folder's earlier name).

## Rendering policy

The components that render (`DocumentComposer`, `PageFileWriter`, `ItemDocumentWriter`, `ItemTextWriter`) take `policy`, a
catalog policy (`id`, default `page-layers`; [catalog](catalog.md#policy-policiesidyaml)), which decides the layer of
each region in the documents, files and texts they write ([data model](data-model.md#rendering)).
`pipelines/transcribe_modular.py` and `pipelines/bind.py` set it with `--policy`; it is a functional parameter, so the
run record names it and `pipeline_sha256` covers it.

<!-- docs/reference/running.md -->

# Running at scale

Where a run runs, how it is divided into tasks and workers, which pages it reads, what it shows while it runs, and
how it gets its credentials and its Jobs. Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s; what a pipeline is made of is in
[pipelines](pipelines.md), fetching over HTTP in [http](http.md).

## Where a run runs

The pipeline is the same everywhere; the command line names the machine.

| Where | Flags |
|---|---|
| this machine | none: the models load inside the pipeline |
| this machine, with a model server | `--backend served`, or `--endpoint URL` for a server that is already up |
| a Ray cluster | `--on ray --tasks 64` |
| Hugging Face Jobs | `--on hf-jobs --namespace NS --commit <sha>` |
| a Slurm cluster | from Python, with datatrove's `SlurmPipelineExecutor` |

On Ray and HF Jobs every task holds one GPU and starts its own model server. A rerun into the same output folder
runs only the tasks that did not finish. The executors behind `--on` are in
[architecture](architecture.md#executors-and-jobs).

### A model server that stays up

A pipeline script serves its own models with `serve`, and a run then names the server's address:

```bash
P="--layout pp-doclayoutv3 --lines pp-ocrv6-medium-det --recognition paddlex-ppocrv6-medium"
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py serve $P
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py scans/ out/ $P --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1
```

A recipe's script serves its models too: `uv run launch.py squiddle serve`, then
`uv run launch.py squiddle scans/ out/ --backend served --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1`. For a vision-language
model, `--recognition-endpoint` points `transcribe_vlm.py` at a running vLLM or SGLang. Servers listen on loopback
only.

### Ray

`ray` runs Ray's own command line with the pipeline's packages, so every machine has the same versions:

```bash
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py ray start --head --num-gpus 8
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py scans/ out/ $P --on ray --tasks 64
```

Images, output and the logging folder must be on storage every machine can reach, such as an `s3://` bucket.

Each task reserves one GPU, `--cpus-per-task` CPUs (default 12) and memory: `--mem-per-cpu-gb` GiB per CPU
(default 4, so 48 GiB), or `--mem-per-task-gb` GiB whatever its CPUs. Start every worker with at least that much
(`ray start --num-cpus`, `--memory`, `--num-gpus`). Before it submits anything, a launch checks that a live node can
run a task, and stops with what a task needs and what the nodes have. It also logs how many tasks fit at once.
`--no-fit-check` leaves the check out, for a cluster that adds nodes on demand. Each task sizes its thread pools
(OpenMP, BLAS, OpenCV, torch) to its CPUs, not to the machine's.

On Kubernetes, one Deployment can run the head and another the workers:

- Start Ray in each pod through the pipeline script (`uv run pipelines/<script>.py ray start …`), so the pods run
  the script's locked packages.
- Give each worker pod the CPUs, memory and GPU a task reserves, plus room for `/dev/shm` (Ray's object store),
  and pass the same amounts to `ray start --num-cpus/--memory/--num-gpus`. A pod with one GPU holds one task.
- With the data on object storage the pods need only ephemeral storage: the environment, the model weights and
  Ray's temporary files.
- Submit the run to the head with `ray job submit`, so it runs inside the cluster and outlives the session that
  submitted it. A driver outside the cluster must reach every node.

### Hugging Face Jobs

Each Job has one GPU and installs linecaster at a pushed commit with the pipeline's pinned dependencies:

```bash
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py s3://<bucket>/images hf://buckets/<ns>/<bucket>/<run> $P \
  --paths-file hf://buckets/<ns>/<bucket>/pages.txt --env FSSPEC_S3_ANON=true \
  --on hf-jobs --namespace NS --commit <sha> --tasks 4000 --workers 64
```

`--workers` Jobs run at once. `--flavor l4x4 --gpus 4` runs four tasks per Job. `--dry-run` launches nothing.
How a Job gets its dependencies is in [HF Jobs helpers](#hf-jobs-helpers).

### Slurm

A `Pipeline`'s components run on a Slurm cluster through datatrove's Slurm executor: one array job, one GPU per
task, in an environment that has the engines (`venv_path`):

```python
from datatrove.executor import SlurmPipelineExecutor

SlurmPipelineExecutor(
    pipeline.steps(), tasks=64, time="04:00:00", partition="gpu",
    gpus_per_task=1, venv_path="/path/to/venv",
    logging_dir="out/logs").run()
```

## Large collections

For a large collection, fetch the images once, then transcribe them, then bind the pages into items. Each
pipeline reads the page records the one before it wrote:

```bash
uv run pipelines/harvest.py --manifests items.parquet --manifest-key url OUT --rate-limit 5/1
uv run pipelines/transcribe_modular.py --pages OUT/pages OUT2 --layout pp-doclayoutv3 \
  --lines pp-ocrv6-medium-det --recognition paddlex-ppocrv6-medium --item-shards 64
uv run pipelines/bind.py OUT2/pages OUT3 --paragraphs unicode-paragraphs --document linked-document \
  --text literal:txt --text latin-historic+flow:md
```

The harvest writes each item's images into a folder of its own and one page record per page. `--item-shards`
writes each item whole into one shard, which `bind.py` reads ([the item stage](pipelines.md#the-item-stage)).

## Samples

A run reads a **sample** of its input with a sample rule: `--sample N` (at most N pages in all), `--sample-per-item K`
(at most K pages of each item), `--sample-items M` (at most M items), `--sample-seed S` (default 0); any of the first
three alone or together. The sample is chosen by the ids of the input's listing alone, before any image is read or
fetched, and is the same whatever `--tasks`, executor or machine: an evaluation then scores every system on the same
pages, and others can recompute them from the list of ids without linecaster.

The rule (`linecaster.data.sample`, `linecaster.sample/1`), with `H(s)` the first 8 bytes of `sha256(s)` (UTF-8) as
an unsigned big-endian integer:

1. The listing is the input's distinct `(item_id, page_id)` pairs; a page without item has the item id `""`. An id
   with a tab is an error.
2. Items are ordered by `(H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}"), item_id)` (the **item rank**), and only the first M are kept.
   An item without pages takes no rank.
3. Within an item, pages are ordered by `(H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}\t{page_id}"), page_id)` (the **page rank**), and
   only the first K are kept; an item with fewer pages gives them all.
4. The pages, in the order (item rank, page rank), are cut after the first N.

The page hash includes the item, so items whose pages are named alike (`0001.png` in every item folder) do not all
give the same positions. A rank depends only on its ids and the seed: an item added to the input moves no other
item's pages, and a sample of N is the first N pages of a sample of 2N. With K the first N pages come from about N/K
items. In Python:

```python
import hashlib

def h(*ids):
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256("\t".join(map(str, ids)).encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

def sample(pairs, seed=0, n=None, k=None, m=None):
    items = {}
    for i, p in dict.fromkeys(pairs): items.setdefault(i, []).append(p)
    order = sorted(items, key=lambda i: (h(seed, i), i))[:m]
    return [(i, p) for i in order for p in sorted(items[i], key=lambda p: (h(seed, i, p), p))[:k]][:n]
```

The first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 sort as `H` does, so SQL can order by them. A stratum is a separate run over
a filtered input.

**Per input** (the readers' `sample`, `linecaster.components.readers.sampling`):

| Input | Ids | Read before the sample | The tasks |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMAGES (`--item-from-parent` for items) | the parent folder, the file name without extension | the file listing | the sample's files in turn |
| `--parquet` (`--item-key` for items) | `--id-key`, or `<item>_<0001>` from `--item-key` and `--sequence-key` | the id columns only | the sample's rows in equal shards (by item with `task_per_item`); a row's image is read with the other sample rows of its row group |
| `--manifests` | the item id of each entry, `<item>_<0001>` for its pages | the item ids; then the manifests of the items in rank order, as far as the rule reaches (every one with `--sample-per-item` alone) | the sample's items as the entries would be; only their sample pages' images are requested |
| `--pages` | `page.item_id`, `id` | every record (no image) | their files as without a sample, passing on the sample's records alone |

`--sample-per-item` and `--sample-items` need items. An id listed twice is read once (its first entry), counted in
the record's `duplicates`. With `--manifests` the manifests the sample reads are saved to `OUT/manifests/` with an
index (`sample.jsonl`: item id, entry, the URL it was read from, the copy's file, its pages); the tasks read those
copies instead of fetching them again, and so does a resume when it computes the sample again. A manifest that
cannot be read, or a IIIF Collection entry, stops the launch: the sample would depend on it. `--max-pages` and a
sample exclude each other; `--limit` and `--skip` still count per task, over the task's share.

The launch computes the sample once, before the tasks (`linecaster.execution.run.sampled`); it travels with the pickled
pipeline, and each task takes its share. It is recorded in the run record's `sample` section:

| Field | Holds |
|---|---|
| `rule`, `hash` | `linecaster.sample/1` and the hashes in words |
| `pages`, `items`, `per_item`, `seed` | N, M, K and S |
| `listing` | `scope` (`pages`, or `items` for manifests, whose pages are known once read), `items`, `pages`, `duplicates`, `manifests_read`, `sha256`: of the distinct sorted lines `item_id<TAB>page_id` (for manifests `item_id`), each with a newline |
| `selected` | `items`, `pages`, `sha256`: of the sample's lines `item_id<TAB>page_id` in sample order, each with a newline |
| `file` | `sample.parquet` |

`OUT/sample.parquet` (`linecaster.execution.sample`) holds one row per sample page in sample order: `rank` (1-based: a
sample of N is `rank <= N`), `item_id`, `page_id`, `item_rank`, `page_rank`, `item_hash`, `page_hash` (unsigned 64
bit) and `item_pages` (the item's pages in the listing), with the record's section in the file's metadata
(`linecaster.sample`). The same sample gives the same rows and metadata, and with the same pyarrow the same bytes;
`selected.sha256` compares samples across versions. `linecaster sample [IMAGES] OUT` with the input and
sample options writes it without a run (with `--manifests`, the manifests too), as a run with the same options would.
A sample's options are operational parameters (the pipeline's hash leaves them out); a resume with another sample is
refused.

## Tasks, workers and rate limits

`--tasks` and `--workers` are chosen when the command line leaves them open (`linecaster.execution.run.allocate`):

| Pipeline | `--tasks` | `--workers` |
|---|---|---|
| with engines | 1 | every task |
| without engines, every rate-limited host through proxies (`--proxies`, an HTTP policy's `proxies: {file}`), local or Ray (`--on hf-jobs`: as below) | the reader's `auto_tasks` (from the input), else 1 | sharing them fairly (`proxies: {per_worker: share}`, the default): one per available proxy, at most one per CPU; with `per_worker` 1 or N: one per available proxy divided by N (`ceil(available / N)`), not capped by the CPUs; either way at most the tasks and, with OUT on object storage, at most 64 (`OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS`) |
| without engines, with `--rate-limit` (a host with rate limits and no proxies) | the reader's `auto_tasks`, else 1 | 1 |
| without engines, without `--rate-limit` | the reader's `auto_tasks`, else 1 | one per CPU, at most the tasks |

The available proxies are counted once at launch from one listing of the broker
(`linecaster.execution.run.available_proxies`): those in the file, less those with a live block or broken mark for the
run's hosts (any host when the hosts are not named in an HTTP policy) and those leased by live workers of other runs
(the run's own earlier leases count as available); on a first launch, without a broker yet, all of them. Sharing
the proxies fairly, a few workers use them all, so their count stops at the CPUs; with one proxy per worker (or up to
N) using them all takes a worker per proxy (per N), and the workers mostly wait on the network, so their count is not
capped by the CPUs. With OUT on object storage (any fsspec protocol but a local one: `s3://`, `gs://`, `hf://`,
`az://`, ...) the count stops at `linecaster.execution.run.OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS` (64) in both modes: in one setup,
250 workers writing to S3-compatible object storage hung in their listings of `OUT/images` and fetched less than 64
did, which ran cleanly; an observation from that setup, not a guarantee for others. The run states the count and why
(`linecaster.execution.run.workers_note`, e.g. `250 proxies available, OUT on object storage → 64 workers, a fair
share each`, or `250 proxies available → 250 workers, 1 proxy each`). `--workers` overrides it (each worker is a
process with its own memory).

`auto_tasks` is about 1,000 pages per task for `ImageParquetReader` and about 5 items per task for `ManifestReader`
(`linecaster.components.readers.tables.PAGES_PER_TASK`, `ITEMS_PER_TASK`), so a resume repeats little. The harvest
(`pipelines/harvest.py`) asks its reader for one item per task (`task_per_item`): the tasks divide the items, an
item's rows wherever they are in the table (`tables.item_runs`), so every item is whole in its task and a task that
fails costs one item. With `--reuse` (off by default: on some object storage a listing is slow even for an empty
folder, and only the items a stopped launch was in, or with `--retry-failed` the finished items with failed pages,
have anything to reuse) its reader also gets `reuse_folder`
(`OUT/images`): when it reaches an item it lists the item's
folder once (an fsspec listing) and reads a page whose image file is already there from the storage instead of
fetching it from the source (`linecaster.components.readers.existing`); only pages of interrupted items (and of the items
`--retry-failed` runs again, whose failed pages alone are then fetched) are read back, so egress stays small. The reader waits at most `LISTING_TIMEOUT` (60 s) for a listing (on object storage fsspec cancels
it then on its IO loop): one that times out or fails is a warning and a stat (`reuse_listing_timeouts`,
`reuse_listing_errors`), and the item's pages are fetched again, their files overwritten. Such a record is complete and says `image.extra.reused`; the console counts it as done but not in
the rate. On a restart the console's size starts with the finished tasks' `media_size` from datatrove's stats files
(`linecaster.execution.local.size_before`, read in the background). Parquet tables are
divided over the tasks by rows in equal shards, not by files, so a table never needs splitting for a task count.
`--max-pages N` (`--parquet`, IMAGES; the readers' `max_pages`) reads the input as if it ended after its first N
pages, in the same automatic tasks: a smoke test of the real setup. `--limit` counts per task, as in datatrove. The
same pages for every setup and input order: a [sample](#samples).

`--rate-limit` holds per worker: each worker process has one fetcher with its limits (`HTTPFetcher.shared`), so a
server sees the workers running at once times the limits; the run states it before it starts
(`linecaster.execution.run.rate_note`, e.g. `rate limits per worker: 150/60, 3/1 · 1 worker → up to 150/min at a
server`). One worker keeps any rate limit busy: a reader's requests ahead grow while none waits for the limits
(`linecaster.net.http.prefetched`, at most `MAX_AHEAD`), and the fetcher, with its limits and the window it has
grown to, is shared by the tasks a worker runs one after the other (`HTTPFetcher.shared`). With `--proxies` the
limits hold per proxy instead (below), and the run states that (`rate limits per proxy: 150/60 · 100 proxies → up to
15,000/min at a server`; with fewer workers than proxies `· 10 of 100 proxies in use (1 proxy per worker)`).

**Proxies.** `--proxies FILE` sends the http(s) requests through a list of proxies, shared by the workers through the
[broker](broker.md) (`--broker PATH`, any fsspec folder, default `OUT/logs/broker`; runs pointed at one path share
the proxies and their blocks too). Each proxy has one worker at a time, the one that holds its lease, and each worker
holds a fair share of them (`linecaster.net.proxies.ProxyPool`, `per_worker: share`, the default): of the
proxies not blocked for the host, divided by the live workers, claimed at most 2 at a time and grown by rebalancing,
which also gives back what is beyond it when another worker joins. An HTTP policy's `proxies: {per_worker: ...}` (per
host or at the root; hosts that share a list share the setting) gives a worker one proxy instead (`1`: it claims a
free one usable for the host and, when that one is blocked or broken, releases it and claims another at once), or up to N,
claimed one by one; with output on local disk or a short list, one per worker and a worker per proxy is the simplest
way to use them all. The host's rate limits hold per
proxy, so per IP, as servers count them: the owner spaces the requests through a proxy to a host by the strictest
limit, and each request goes through the owned proxy whose turn comes first. A proxy is left out when the failure is
its own ([http](http.md#blocks)). A block (a status in the host's `block_on`, 429 by default, and with `html` there an
HTML page where another format was expected) is a mark in the broker for that host, until its `Retry-After`, else for
60 s, doubling on each repeat up to the host's `block_ttl` (an hour by default): the owner stops using the proxy there
at once, releases it once it is blocked for every host it uses, and whoever claims it later sees the mark, so no
worker sends a request into another's block, and a restarted run none into a block it found before. A broken proxy (a
proxy error, no connection to it, `broken_after` failures in a row, 3 by default) is marked for every host, first for
`broken_ttl` (5 minutes), doubling up to `block_ttl`. A block does not count as an attempt and the request goes on
through another proxy at once, so `max_retries` (retries after the first attempt) counts only the attempts that
reached the server and failed there; a component does not count toward the breaker either. A timeout is mostly a slow
server: it is retried and leaves the proxy in. When none of a worker's proxies is usable for a host and none
is free to claim, its requests to the host pause until a block ends or another worker gives a proxy back (one warning
when the pause starts, one when it ends; the wait is in the fetch record's `pause_seconds`); once the waits since the
host's last successful response would pass its `max_pause` (6 hours; [http](http.md#max_pause)) the run stops
(`StopRequests`) and says when the first proxy returns. An HTTP policy
can set `proxies: {block_ttl: 72h, broken_after: 1}` and further statuses that block at the host (`block_on: [429,
403]`, `block_on: [429, html]`). The console shows the proxies the worker holds, those blocked and those free. On Ray
each task is a process of its own; the next task on a machine takes over the worker slot the last one handed over, and
with it its proxies. The file holds one proxy per line, a URL or `host:port[:user:pass]` as Webshare lists them; the
run record keeps its name, logs show proxies without credentials (`linecaster.net.http.redact`), and the broker names
them by a hash of host and port.

**Failures.** Each fetcher has a breaker (`linecaster.net.http.Breaker`): when most attempts of the last minute got a
server error (5xx, Cloudflare's 520-524 among them), its requests pause, a probe goes out now and then (waits doubling
from one to ten minutes), and the first answer that is not a server error lets them go on; the pages wait instead of
failing. A single server error is retried (with a proxy list without counting against the proxy it came through). A
block on a direct connection (a status in the host's `block_on`, 429 by default) pauses the worker that got it
(`linecaster.net.http.Pause`): its requests to that host wait until the response's `Retry-After` has passed (seconds
or an HTTP-date; without one a minute, doubling while components keep coming), then the request that got it is tried
again, without using up one of its retries; blocks for requests already in flight extend the pause, never shorten
it. The pages wait instead of failing, and the requests to other hosts and other workers go on. The log says when a pause starts (host,
status, how long, until when) and when the requests go on, and a page's fetch record has the time paused
(`pause_seconds`). A worker that would pause more than the host's `max_pause` (6 hours) since its last successful
response stops the run: the worker waits, or stops when the wait would be too long ([http](http.md#max_pause), one
count for both paths). Through proxies a block leaves
that proxy out at the host instead (above). An HTML page where an image, XML or JSON was expected is a failed attempt,
retried like a server error, unless the host's policy makes it a block or a stop ([http](http.md#unexpected-html)). A
local task that fails is logged and the others go on (`LocalExecutor`); it runs again on the next launch. An error
that is not the pages' (`NOT_THE_PAGES`) or `FAILED_IN_A_ROW` failed tasks in a row in one worker stop the run.
`--retry-failed` runs the finished tasks that left rejects again; `kill -USR1 <pid>` dumps every thread's stack.
On Ray (`linecaster.execution.ray.RayExecutor`) the same error stops the run through a marker in the logging folder
(`stopped.json`): every task after it ends before its pipeline starts, so none sends a request into the component that
stopped the first, and the launch fails with that task's error; a launch that left tasks unfinished fails too, so the
Ray job does not end as succeeded. A new launch removes the marker. Before it submits a task, a Ray launch checks
that a live node has what a task reserves (`--cpus-per-task`; `--mem-per-task-gb`, else `--mem-per-cpu-gb` per CPU;
one GPU for a stage with models) and stops with a `PipelineConfigError` if none has, where Ray would keep the tasks
waiting without an error; `--no-fit-check` leaves the check out, for a cluster that adds nodes on demand. A task sizes
the native thread pools to the CPUs it may use (`linecaster.execution.cpus`: its Ray CPUs, else the cgroup's CPU quota),
and so do the worker counts a launch derives "one per CPU".

**Resources.** `pipelines/harvest.py --items TABLE --item-key COL` fetches items' remote files other than page images
(`ResourceReader`): from URL templates per kind (`--resource marcxml=https://catalog.example.org/{item}/marcxml`) or
a table with one row per resource (`--url-key`, `--kind-key`, `--name-key`). Each is checked (XML, JSON or an image must parse, a DjVu file must start with its signature;
an HTML page where another format was expected is retried, and a resource that fails with it counts toward the
breaker) and kept as a raw copy,
`OUT/<kind>/<item>/<name>.<ext>` (`ResourceFilesWriter`), the reference later stages link to, with its fetch record in
`OUT/resources/<rank>.jsonl.gz` (`ResourceRecordWriter`: source and final URL, status, type, size, `sha256`, ETag,
Last-Modified, time). One item per task, `--max-items` for a smoke test, copies already there read back. `--http-policy FILE`
gives the run's requests their settings from one YAML file (`linecaster.net.policy`, [http](http.md#the-http-policy)):
for every host at the root, and under `hosts:` an entry for each host that differs, whose fields replace the root's;
the run's own options go between the two. The settings: rate limits (per proxy through proxies), retries
(`max_retries`), deadline, User-Agent, what blocks (`block_on`, default `[429]`; with `html` an HTML page where
another format was expected) and what stops the run without a retry (`stop_on`: statuses and `html`; something in
both `block_on`, or its default, and `stop_on` is refused, so `block_on: []` with `stop_on: [429]` stops on a 429),
`max_pause`, `direct`, the proxy path's own section (`proxies: {file, per_worker, block_ttl, broken_after,
broken_ttl}`) and the broker (root only). The run states the rules that hold per host before it starts. For every
input fetched over http(s): `--items`, `--parquet` with http(s) image URLs, `--manifests` (the manifests, their
images and OCR files) and `--pages` (the images it fetches again); with rate limits in the file for a host without
proxies a run keeps one worker, with proxies for every rate-limited host its workers follow the available proxies
(above).

The default User-Agent is datatrove's, `HF-Research/1.0` (`linecaster.net.http.USER_AGENT`), deliberately: datatrove
is integral to linecaster, and its media fetcher (`HTTPFetchReader`) sends the same, so a run that fetches through
both presents itself as one client to every host. `--user-agent` or an HTTP policy's `user_agent` sets another.

## The console

A local run (`--on local`, `linecaster.execution.local.LocalExecutor`) shows on the terminal: one line naming the
pipeline (its components, without the builder's boundaries; pages, tasks and workers; what an earlier launch finished), a
live progress line (pages done of the total, rate over the last five minutes, size, failed pages, the task, the time
left) pinned to the terminal's top row, with everything else scrolling below it (a scroll region, `Pinned`), a line per finished task and a summary, in human units
(`linecaster.execution.console`). The `Progress` observer, which the runtime puts on every stage, counts the pages
that leave the pipeline; with several workers each worker process reports its counts to the console about every
second. Off a terminal the progress is a log line every 30 s instead.
datatrove's own console output (its pipeline listing and stats component per task, the merged stats) goes only to the
task logs (`OUT/logs/logs/task_<rank>.log`, in its full line format) and the stats files, which keep it whole. A launch
lists the completion markers once instead of looking them up task by task.

## Secrets

`linecaster.secrets.EnvVar("NAME")` names an environment variable; the value is read in the task
(`resolve()`), never stored: an `EnvVar` pickles by name, `to_dict()` writes `{"env": "NAME"}`.
`Served(endpoint, model, api_key=EnvVar("NAME"), headers={"X-Team": "ocr", "X-Token": EnvVar("TOKEN")})` (and
`Chat(preset, endpoint, api_key=..., headers=...)` alike) sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and the headers with
every request through saturate's `AdaptiveClient(headers=...)`;
a key given as text is refused. A missing variable fails the component's warm-up.

## HF Jobs helpers

A launch with `--on hf-jobs` names `--namespace`, the Hugging Face user or organization the Jobs run under and are
billed to, and `--commit`, the linecaster commit the Jobs install (pushed). Neither has a default, and the namespace
is not taken from the logged-in account, so the account a run spends is always the one its command line and run
record name. `--commit` is required for linecaster's own scripts; a downstream project's script outside the linecaster
checkout that takes linecaster from a git tag, branch or rev runs without it (`jobs.needs_commit`), since its Jobs
install what its sources name.

`linecaster.execution.jobs.dependencies(commit, script=None, engines=True)` spells out what a Job installs from a
pipeline script, linecaster's or a downstream project's, as `Dependencies`:

- `requirements`: the script's dependencies with their sources as PEP 508 URLs (`url` as it is; `git` with its
  `tag`, `branch` or `rev` and its `subdirectory`, as `git+URL@REF#subdirectory=DIR`; a `path` into the linecaster
  checkout as GitHub's source archive of linecaster at `commit`, any other path an error), then every package
  reachable from them in the script's lock that comes from no index (the sources the packages declare themselves:
  the kraken fork at its locked commit, the OpenCV stub);
- `constraints`: every package reachable from them that the lock takes from an index, at the lock's version
  (`name==version`; a package the lock holds at several versions with its resolution markers), so a Job resolves the
  versions of the lock; none for a script without a lock;
- `overrides`: the script's `[tool.uv] override-dependencies` (a lock that resolves only with them, such as
  `transcribe_page.py`'s `pillow==12.3.0` over surya-ocr's `pillow<11`).

linecaster's `ray` extra is left out. `engines=False` keeps linecaster with its extras and the sources they need, and
the constraints of what those reach; without a script it raises unless `engines=False` (linecaster alone). A
downstream project's pipeline runs on Jobs from its own script (its sources pinned to a linecaster tag), read as it is on disk.

`uv run --with` (datatrove's way of installing a Job's dependencies) ignores constraints and overrides, whether given
as `UV_CONSTRAINT`, `UV_OVERRIDE` or a `uv.toml`; only a script's own `[tool.uv]` brings them to `uv run`. So
`JobsExecutor` given `Dependencies` uploads, in place of datatrove's `launch_pickled_pipeline.py`, a uv script of the
same name whose inline metadata holds the requirements, `constraint-dependencies` and `override-dependencies`
(`Dependencies.script`) and which then runs datatrove's launcher. Constraints only bound what the requirements bring:
a package the lock holds for another platform is not installed. `--dry-run` prints the three lists; the run record
keeps them (`dependencies`, `constraints`, `overrides`).

<!-- docs/reference/data-model.md -->

# The data model

`linecaster.data` holds what is read from a page and how it is rendered; `linecaster.data.page` the page record it
travels in. A stored page record names its format in its row's `schema`: `linecaster.page/6`. Importing
`linecaster.data` needs neither datatrove nor saturate nor an engine.

## Principles

1. **Raw output is kept.** What a model answered (a completion, an engine's native result) is stored verbatim, once
   per request, next to what linecaster parsed from it (`RawOutput`).
2. **Nothing is discarded or overwritten.** Every step adds annotations; a correction, a removal, a relabelling is a
   new annotation that refers to the one it is about. A page record holds everything any step said, and who said it.
3. **The record holds the text as read.** A reading is what the model or the source gave, exactly, not even in NFC.
